ourAnswer: Aqueous CuSO4 is [Cu(H2O)4]2+ (blue). (i) F- displaces water to give [CuF4]2-, the green precipitate. (ii) Cl- displaces water to give [CuCl4]2-, the bright green solution. Both colour changes follow from F- and Cl- lying below H2O in the spectrochemical series, so the smaller splitting shifts the d-d absorption.
keyAnswer: Aqueous CuSO4 exists as [Cu(H2O)4]SO4, blue due to [Cu(H2O)4]2+. (i) KF: weak H2O ligands replaced by F- forming [CuF4]2-, a green precipitate. (ii) KCl: Cl- replaces H2O forming [CuCl4]2-, bright green. Both equations given.
note: Same species, same two substitution equations, same conclusion. Our answer additionally supplies the crystal-field reason for the colour change, which the key does not; nothing in it contradicts the key.

ourAnswer: The entity is [Cu(CN)4]3-, tetracyanidocuprate(I): excess CN- both reduces Cu(II) to Cu(I) (evolving cyanogen) and complexes it, 2Cu2+ + 10CN- -> 2[Cu(CN)4]3- + C2N2. No CuS forms because the complex is extremely stable, so the free copper ion concentration never lets the ionic product exceed the solubility product of copper sulphide.
keyAnswer: [Cu(H2O)4]2+ + 4CN- -> [Cu(CN)4]2- + 4H2O. As CN- is a strong ligand it forms a highly stable complex with Cu2+; on passing H2S, free Cu2+ ions are not available to form the precipitate of CuS.
note: DISPUTED ON THE IDENTITY OF THE ENTITY ONLY; the two halves of the question score differently. The key writes the product as [Cu(CN)4]2-, i.e. copper retained in the +2 state. Cyanide is not merely a strong ligand towards copper(II), it is a reducing agent: Cu(II) cyanide is unstable and decomposes with evolution of cyanogen, so the isolable species from excess KCN is the copper(I) complex K3[Cu(CN)4] and the ion is [Cu(CN)4]3-. Tetracyanidocuprate(II) is not a stable species. The SECOND half of the key — that the complex is so stable that free copper ions are unavailable, so no CuS precipitates — is correct and our answer agrees with it. A defensible reading of the key is that it presents a simplified ligand-substitution picture at this level and ignores the redox step; that is for the maintainer to adjudicate. Flagged, not corrected.

ourAnswer: Spectrochemical series defined and quoted; weak field means Delta_o < P (high spin), strong field means Delta_o > P (low spin).
Delta_o defined as the t2g/eg gap; if Delta_o < P the fourth electron enters eg (high spin t2g3 eg1), if Delta_o > P it pairs in t2g (low spin t2g4 eg0).

The aqua ion has a small Delta_o and a partly filled eg set, so it absorbs in the visible and transmits green; the strong-field square planar cyanido ion has all d electrons paired and so large a splitting that absorption falls in the ultraviolet, so it is colourless.

keyAnswer: (i) OS +3, CN 6, t2g6 eg0.  (ii) OS +3, CN 6, d3 (t2g3).  (iii) OS +2, CN 4, d7 (t2g5 eg2).  (iv) OS +2, CN 6, d5 (t2g3 eg2).

Worth recording but NOT scored as a disagreement: for (iii) the key labels a FOUR-coordinate complex's configuration with the octahedral labels 't2g5 eg2'. A tetrahedral field splits the d orbitals into e and t2 (and carries no 'g' subscript, there being no centre of symmetry), so those labels do not belong to a CN = 4 entity. Our answer states the d7 count and CN = 4 without asserting any octahedral split, so it neither repeats nor contradicts the key's notation.

ourAnswer: (i) geometrical (cis/trans) and, for the cis form, optical.  (ii) optical only (d,l) — a [M(AA)3] tris-chelate has one geometrical arrangement.  (iii) linkage (NO2- is ambidentate, -NO2 versus -ONO) and ionisation (coordinated NO2- exchanging with the NO3- counter ion); geometrical isomerism is NOT possible.  (iv) geometrical (cis/trans); neither form is optically active, the entity being square planar.
keyAnswer: (i) Both geometrical (cis-, trans-) and optical isomers for cis can exist.  (ii) Two optical isomers can exist.  (iii) There are 10 possible isomers. (Hint: There are geometrical, ionisation and linkage isomers possible).  (iv) Geometrical (cis-, trans-) isomers can exist.
note: SUB-ITEMS (i), (ii) AND (iv) AGREE EXACTLY. The disagreement is confined to (iii), where the key lists GEOMETRICAL isomerism as possible for [Co(NH3)5(NO2)](NO3)2. That entity is octahedral of the type Ma5b — five identical ammine ligands and one nitrito ligand. All six vertices of an octahedron are equivalent, so placing the odd ligand at any vertex gives the same structure and geometrical isomerism is impossible; only linkage and ionisation isomerism arise, which is what our answer states. The key's count of '10 possible isomers' is not reproducible without the geometrical forms it wrongly admits, and our answer deliberately claims no total (the authoring note recorded that the TYPES, not an exhaustive enumeration, were derived). Flagged, not corrected.

ourAnswer: [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 releases free SO4(2-), so it gives a white BaSO4 precipitate with Ba2+ and none with Ag+; [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Cl releases free Cl-, so it gives white AgCl with Ag+ and none with Ba2+. Different ions in solution, hence different reactions to the same reagents — the evidence for ionisation isomerism.
keyAnswer: The ionisation isomers dissolve in water to yield different ions and thus react differently to various reagents: [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 + Ba2+ -> BaSO4 (s); [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br + Ba2+ -> No reaction; [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 + Ag+ -> No reaction; [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br + Ag+ -> AgBr (s).
note: The reasoning, the reagents and the conclusion are identical, so the row scores AGREE. Worth reporting as a BOOK INCONSISTENCY rather than a wrong answer: the printed question (p-10) asks about the CHLORIDE pair [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 / [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Cl, while the key's worked answer is written for the BROMIDE pair [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 / [Co(NH3)5(SO4)]Br — which is the pair used as the worked illustration of ionisation isomerism in section 5.4.5 on p-09. The key therefore demonstrates the right method on the wrong halide. Our answer follows the question as printed and uses Ag+/AgCl where the key uses Ag+/AgBr.

ourAnswer: In [Ni(CO)4] nickel is in the zero oxidation state (3d8 4s2); CO is strong field so the 4s electrons move into 3d, giving 3d10 with everything paired, sp3 tetrahedral and diamagnetic. In [NiCl4]2- nickel is +2 (3d8) and Cl- is weak field, so two unpaired electrons remain, sp3 tetrahedral and paramagnetic.
keyAnswer: In Ni(CO)4, Ni is in zero oxidation state whereas in NiCl4(2-) it is in +2 oxidation state. In the presence of CO ligand, the unpaired d electrons of Ni pair up but Cl- being a weak ligand is unable to pair up the unpaired electrons.
note: Same two causes — the oxidation state and the ligand field strength — and the same conclusion.

ourAnswer: Both are Fe(III) 3d5. H2O is weak field: no pairing, five unpaired, sp3d2 outer orbital, 5.92 BM, strongly paramagnetic. CN- is strong field: pairing to t2g5, one unpaired, d2sp3 inner orbital, 1.73 BM, weakly paramagnetic.
keyAnswer: In presence of CN- (a strong ligand) the 3d electrons pair up leaving only one unpaired electron. The hybridisation is d2sp3 forming inner orbital complex. In the presence of H2O (a weak ligand), 3d electrons do not pair up. The hybridisation is sp3d2 forming an outer orbital complex containing five unpaired electrons, it is strongly paramagnetic.
note: Identical on the unpaired-electron counts (1 and 5) and on both hybridisations. Our answer additionally quotes the spin-only moments, which the key does not.

ourAnswer: Co3+ is 3d6; NH3 forces the six electrons into the three t2g orbitals, leaving two 3d orbitals empty for d2sp3 — an inner orbital complex. Ni2+ is 3d8; even with maximum pairing two electrons remain in the eg set, so no two 3d orbitals can be vacated and hybridisation must use the outer 4d orbitals, sp3d2 — an outer orbital complex.
keyAnswer: In the presence of NH3, the 3d electrons pair up leaving two d orbitals empty to be involved in d2sp3 hybridisation forming inner orbital complex in case of [Co(NH3)6]3+. In Ni(NH3)6(2+), Ni is in +2 oxidation state and has d8 configuration, the hybridisation involved is sp3d2 forming outer orbital complex.
note: Same mechanism and same two hybridisations. Our answer states in addition WHY the d8 ion cannot vacate two 3d orbitals, which the key leaves implicit.

ourAnswer: Pt2+ is 5d8; a square planar shape requires dsp2, so the 5d electrons pair to vacate one 5d orbital, leaving all eight paired. Number of unpaired electrons = 0, so the ion is diamagnetic.
keyAnswer: For square planar shape, the hybridisation is dsp2. Hence the unpaired electrons in 5d orbital pair up to make one d orbital empty for dsp2 hybridisation. Thus there is no unpaired electron.
note: Identical reasoning and identical answer of zero unpaired electrons.
